passages.t: The king's heart in the LORD's hand
passages.happening:
“The king’s heart is a waterway in the hand of the LORD; He directs it where He pleases” (verse 1). ‘All a man’s ways seem right to him, but the LORD weighs the heart’ (verse 2). ‘To do righteousness and justice is more desirable to the LORD than sacrifice’ (verse 3). Haughty eyes and a proud heart are sin (verse 4).

‘The plans of the diligent bring plenty, as surely as haste leads to poverty’ (verse 5). ‘Making a fortune by a lying tongue is a vanishing mist, a deadly pursuit’ (verse 6). ‘The violence of the wicked will sweep them away because they refuse to do what is just’ (verse 7). ‘The way of a guilty man is crooked, but the conduct of the innocent is upright’ (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
Verse 1 uses the picture of irrigation. In Egypt, Mesopotamia and the gardens of Israel, farmers dug small channels from a water source and turned the flow by opening or blocking them, sometimes with a foot or a hoe. The water goes wherever the farmer turns it. So the LORD turns the heart of the most powerful man in the land, not by overriding it, but as easily as a gardener guides water.

The book has set human plans under God's rule again and again (16:1, 9; 19:21; 20:24). This chapter takes that to the highest human point, the king, and ends with the most dangerous human enterprise, war. No one stands outside God's rule.

Verse 3 speaks the language of the prophets and of Samuel. Proverbs does not reject temple worship, but like the prophets it insists that sacrifice cannot take the place of justice.
passages.later: The Bible shows the LORD turning a king's heart: ‘the LORD stirred the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia to send a proclamation throughout his kingdom’ (Ezra 1:1), and the exiles went home. And the prophet Micah sums up verse 3: “He has shown you, O man, what is good. And what does the LORD require of you but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?” (Micah 6:8).
passages.asks: The LORD weighs the heart, not only the outward act. Ask where you are offering God something on the surface while avoiding the justice or kindness he actually asks. And ask what plan you are rushing that patience would serve better.

passages.t: A corner of the roof, the cry of the poor, and a hard saying
passages.happening:
‘Better to live on a corner of the roof than to share a house with a quarrelsome wife’ (verse 9). ‘The soul of the wicked man craves evil; his neighbor finds no favor in his eyes’ (verse 10).

“Whoever shuts his ears to the cry of the poor, he too shall cry out and receive no answer” (verse 13). ‘A gift in secret soothes anger, and a covert bribe pacifies great wrath’ (verse 14). ‘Justice executed is a joy to the righteous, but a terror to the workers of iniquity’ (verse 15).

‘He who loves pleasure will become poor; the one who loves wine and oil will never be rich’ (verse 17). ‘The wicked become a ransom for the righteous, and the faithless for the upright’ (verse 18). ‘Better to live in the desert than with a contentious and ill-tempered wife’ (verse 19).
passages.hearers:
Israelite houses had flat roofs used for storage, drying crops and sleeping in hot weather. Living on a corner of the roof meant exposure to sun and rain, and living in the desert meant exile from the community. Verses 9 and 19 are exaggerations that say how miserable a home without peace can be. The same thought comes in 19:13, 25:24 and 27:15. They are not a comment on women in general. The book calls a prudent wife a gift from the LORD (19:14), and it warns just as plainly about angry men. These sayings give no one a license for contempt.

If you are being hurt, at home, at work or in a church, tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

Verse 13 is one of the book's sternest warnings. Whoever will not hear the poor will one day cry out and not be heard.

Verse 14 describes, it does not commend. A secret gift can calm an angry man, as Jacob's gifts calmed Esau. The book elsewhere condemns the bribe that bends justice (17:23).
passages.later: Isaiah promises the opposite of verse 13 to those who care for the needy: ‘Then you will call, and the LORD will answer’ (Isaiah 58:9). And Esther shows the reversal of verse 18: ‘So they hanged Haman on the gallows he had prepared for Mordecai’ (Esther 7:10).
passages.hard:
What does verse 18 mean when it says the wicked become a ransom for the righteous?

The verse is puzzling, because elsewhere in Scripture a ransom is paid by one party to free another, and it is hard to see how the wicked could pay anything for the righteous.

Most interpreters read it in light of 11:8, which says the righteous are delivered from trouble and the wicked go in their place. On this reading the saying describes a reversal: the disaster that threatened the righteous falls instead on the wicked, as when Haman was hanged on the gallows he had built for Mordecai (Esther 7:10). The word ransom is used loosely, for one taking another's place in trouble.

Some readers see a broader principle: when God judges, the guilty bear the penalty they tried to bring on the innocent. That is also the logic of the law about a false witness (Deuteronomy 19:19).
passages.asks: The chapter warns about shutting your ears to the poor. Ask whose cry you have learned not to hear. And ask what it would take to make your own home a place of peace, not a house anyone would rather leave.

passages.t: No plan against the LORD, and victory is his
passages.happening:
‘Precious treasures and oil are in the dwelling of the wise, but a foolish man consumes them’ (verse 20). ‘He who pursues righteousness and loving devotion finds life, righteousness, and honor’ (verse 21). ‘A wise man scales the city of the mighty and pulls down the stronghold in which they trust’ (verse 22). ‘He who guards his mouth and tongue keeps his soul from distress’ (verse 23).

‘The craving of the slacker kills him because his hands refuse to work’ (verse 25). ‘All day long he covets more, but the righteous give without restraint’ (verse 26). A sacrifice of the wicked is detestable, and still worse when brought with evil intent (verse 27).

The chapter ends with God. “There is no wisdom, no understanding, no counsel that can prevail against the LORD” (verse 30). “A horse is prepared for the day of battle, but victory is of the LORD” (verse 31).
passages.hearers:
Verses 25 and 26 form a pair: the slacker craves endlessly and does nothing, and the righteous give without holding back. The contrast is not between rich and poor but between grasping and giving.

Verse 27 sharpens verse 3. A sacrifice brought with evil intent may be an attempt to buy God's favor for a wrong someone is planning. That is worse than empty worship.

Horses in the ancient world mostly pulled war chariots, and they were costly symbols of power. The law warned Israel's king not to pile up horses, yet Solomon built a great chariot force. Verse 31 does not forbid preparing for battle. It forbids trusting in the preparation. Verse 30's triple ‘no’ gives the chapter's last word great force: nothing prevails against the LORD.
passages.later: The psalms say it the same way: ‘Some trust in chariots and others in horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God’ (Psalm 20:7), and ‘A horse is a vain hope for salvation’ (Psalm 33:17).
passages.asks: The horse is ready, and the victory is the LORD's. Ask what you have prepared carefully and then trusted more than God. And ask where you could give without restraint this week, instead of craving more.
